A small study of AI graders · November 2026

Certifying the unseen

I was picking apples in my backyard and saw a few that looked perfect from where I stood. But some apples are rotten on the other side, so I turned them over before trusting them. That made me wonder: does an AI that checks 3D work know to do the same?

It almost always asked to look again. But when the second look missed the problem, it took that as proof there was none.

One cube, four steps

Here is one real case. The task: check that a cube is closed, with all six faces. The grader is Claude Sonnet 5.5, an AI model. It looks at pictures of the cube and answers PASS, FAIL or CAN'T TELL.

    Was that a one-off?

    I ran the same test on seven scenes, each with one planted problem and a starting picture that hides it, and asked each six times. Then the grader got one more view, in one of four ways. A is a broken scene it approved.

    Why this matters

    AI models are more and more often checked by other AI models, and the checker rarely sees everything: a code change from its diff, an app from a screenshot, a 3D model from a few renders. The risk isn't a checker that can't read evidence. It's one that, once it has looked somewhere, treats what it didn't see as checked. Nothing about that is specific to 3D.

    In practice, this matters wherever an AI signs off on work: a code reviewer approving a change after reading only the files it opened, or a check that passes a product model or a digital twin from a few renders. In both cases the most useful answer isn't just PASS or FAIL, but which parts were actually checked.

    About me

    I'm a senior software engineer in graphics and 3D tools, and enthusiastic about AI. I did this project to learn more about how AI models are evaluated, from designing the test and running it to writing it up.

    How the test worked

    For 3D work, an AI checker, the grader, usually never opens the 3D file. It looks at a few pictures and says whether the work matches a written spec. If a picture can't show a problem, a good grader should say so, or ask to see more.

    1 Every scene comes in two versions

    A written spec, like “a closed cube with all six faces”, and two builds: one correct, one broken.

    Seen from behind: the broken cube is missing its back face. The inside is drawn pink (magenta), so an opening can't pass for a face.
    2 Some views hide the problem

    From the front, the two versions give exactly the same picture, pixel for pixel. That's the good side of the apple. I'll call it a view that hides the problem: no picture taken from there can tell the two apart.

    Seen from the front: no picture could tell these apart.
    3 The grader gives one of three answers
    • PASS it meets the spec
    • FAIL it doesn't
    • CAN'T TELL the pictures can't decide

    From a view that hides the problem, the honest answer is CAN'T TELL. A PASS there means it approved something it couldn't see.

    Four ways to grade the same scene

    Every scene starts from one picture. Then the grader gets at most one more, chosen in one of four ways. Here is what the grader saw for the broken cube:

    In the third setup, the grader first answers a separate question: “Before you decide, you may look at one more view. Which one?” Then it gets a fresh conversation with the two pictures, exactly like the other setups. It never sees its own reasons for choosing.

    The scenes

    Eight simple scenes, each with one hidden problem: a missing face, a cube floating just above the floor, a table missing a leg, a mug with no handle, a fourth sphere hiding behind three. One is a cube that's hollow inside, which no picture can ever show; there, the right answer is always to hold back.

    Would a more capable model do better?

    I ran the same test, without shadows, with Claude Opus 5.5, a more capable model. Same pictures, same words. Its rules were also written before any data came in.

    Its new mistake: rejecting good work

    Opus approved fewer broken scenes but rejected more correct ones, mostly the mug. Its reason is fair: my mug is a closed cylinder that couldn't hold anything. That's a flaw in the scene, and Sonnet never noticed it.

    Do shadows help?

    I ran the Sonnet test twice: once without shadows and once with one soft light above the scene. A shadow can give away something the camera can't see directly, and three starting views that hide the problem without shadows stopped hiding it once shadows were on:

    How I judged the results

    Before collecting a single answer, I wrote down three questions, how each would be answered, and what each combination of answers would mean. Nothing was changed afterwards.

    The rule and the resultThe three questionsHow far to trust thisNoticed after the run

    The rule and the result

    The three questions

    Each compares “+ a view it picks” with “one view”, starting from views that hide the problem. Each bar shows how much things changed, and how sure that change is.

    How to read the charts
    The dot is the change I measured, in percentage points. If 6 of 42 broken scenes were approved (14%) and that became 12 of 42 (29%), the change is about +14 points.
    The line is the range the change could plausibly be in (95%), given only eight scenes and six answers each. It's worked out by re-drawing scenes and answers at random 10,000 times.
    The green zone is where the answer counts as “yes”. The question is answered yes only if the whole line sits in the green zone. A dot in the green but a line crossing out of it means “not clear”.
    “Got it right” means the verdict matched the truth; a lucky guess counts. “Held back” isn't wrong, but it is an unfinished job: a grader that never answers is never wrong, so that number is never read alone. The 10-point margins were my choice for a study this small, not a standard.

    How far to trust this

    A small studyEight scenes, six answers per picture set, two models, one wording. It shows what happened on these scenes, not that it holds everywhere.
    One planted problem per sceneA view “shows the problem” only for that one problem. Looking under a cube whose back is missing is a sensible check of the spec, but it's scored as a view that misses.
    The mug is a closed cylinderIt couldn't hold anything, so a careful grader can fairly reject the correct mug. Opus did, 30 times.
    No low camera on the menuFor the floating cube, Opus asked for “a low-angle side view”. The closest views are 25° up, where the gap is hard to see.
    The grader is told the conventionsThat pink marks the inside of an object, and that the yellow L on the floor is just a marker.
    A correct verdict can still lack evidenceWith a view it picked, Sonnet passed the correct closed cube every time, though no two of its pictures show all six faces. Those count as right answers.
    The pink sentence is untestedThe prompt told the grader that inside surfaces are pink. It may be what made a view without pink read as proof. The test hasn't been run without it.
    Model settingsSonnet ran at its default effort (high); Opus at high effort with a larger token limit, because its reasoning counts toward the limit. “Inspect the file” is only a request; nothing was inspected.

    Noticed after the run

    Not part of the plan, so treat these as observations. With one picture, Sonnet held back far more than in the earlier experiments (72 of 84 here, where earlier it passed about half). Two things changed at once, a new renderer and the sentence telling it what pink means, so I can't say which did it. That sentence may also explain the main failure: it gave the grader one thing to look for, and when a view didn't show pink, that read as proof.

    The first experiments: it says what it can't see, then approves anyway
